questions.title: Why could the Second Circuit decide fair use on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without discovery?
questions.question_body: The panel says fair use may be "so clearly established by a complaint" as to support dismissal at the pleading stage (citing TCA Television). Here, the court relied on the videos and the broadcast segments themselves. How does the incorporation-by-reference/judicial notice doctrine let the court look past the complaint’s characterizations and evaluate the works directly without converting to summary judgment? What are the limits on doing this, especially when transformative purpose turns on a "reasonable observer" standard after Warhol?

questions.title: How did the court treat Santos’s claim that Kimmel ‘instigated’ the creation of the videos when analyzing transformative use?
questions.question_body: Santos argued that because Kimmel submitted the prompts, he effectively designed the videos’ original purpose, undermining a finding of transformation. The court rejected this, emphasizing an objective reasonable-observer perspective under Warhol. Why doesn’t the requester’s role in shaping the original work’s content defeat a finding that the later broadcast use had a different purpose or character? Are there cases where the instigator’s role does matter to the first fair-use factor?

questions.title: Does alleged bad faith or deception in obtaining a copy negate fair use after Campbell and Google v. Oracle?
questions.question_body: Santos argued Kimmel’s use of aliases on Cameo showed bad faith that should weigh against fair use (citing Harper & Row's 'good faith' language). The panel called that language questionable after Campbell and Google v. Oracle and found the complaint showed a purpose of commentary/criticism. In practical terms, does deception ever meaningfully tip the first factor or overall balance against fair use in the Second Circuit, and what kind of record would be needed for that?

questions.title: Why did commentary about Santos’s behavior (not the works themselves) still count as ‘transformative’ commentary?
questions.question_body: The opinion frames the JKL segments’ purpose as commenting on Santos’s willingness to "say absurd things for money," which targets Santos rather than critiquing the expressive content of each Cameo video. Under Campbell, parody targets the original work, while satire can be more attenuated. How does Second Circuit law treat commentary that uses a work to criticize the subject or creator rather than the work’s expression—why is that still sufficiently transformative here?

questions.title: How did the court handle the third fair-use factor when Kimmel allegedly used the entirety of the Cameo videos?
questions.question_body: The opinion does not dwell on factor three, but it seems the show aired full videos or substantial portions. In Second Circuit practice, when is taking an entire work permissible because it is 'reasonable in relation to the purpose' (e.g., for commentary or criticism)? What reasoning would justify minimal discussion of factor three here?

questions.title: Why did the court find no cognizable market harm under factor four despite Santos’s claim of lost licensing value?
questions.question_body: The panel says we ask whether the secondary use 'usurps the market ... by offering a competing substitute' (citing Hachette) and notes Campbell’s point that creators are unlikely to license criticism. If Santos sells Cameo videos for money, why doesn’t a broadcast that repurposes them for ridicule count as market substitution or at least impairment of a derivative licensing market? What makes the JKL use non-substitutable for buyers of Cameo videos?

questions.title: How did the court determine that the Cameo videos were 'published,' and why does that matter to factor two?
questions.question_body: The court took judicial notice of copyright registrations showing the videos were published the same day they were created and cited the §101 definition. Is it proper to treat statements on the registration about publication as true at the 12(b)(6) stage, or just notice of what the registration asserts? Do privately delivered, paywalled Cameo videos qualify as 'published' under §101, and how does their being published affect the factor-two analysis?

questions.title: Why didn’t the court reach any First Amendment analysis beyond fair use?
questions.question_body: Given the expressive, critical nature of the JKL segments, I expected a First Amendment discussion. Instead, the court treats fair use as dispositive. Is fair use considered the constitutional accommodation for speech interests within copyright, making separate First Amendment balancing unnecessary unless fair use is inadequate? Under what circumstances would the Second Circuit add a First Amendment layer beyond the §107 analysis?

questions.title: What is the Second Circuit’s appellate jurisdictional basis here, and could the panel affirm on alternative grounds not reached below?
questions.question_body: The opinion summarily affirms the 12(b)(6) dismissal and says it 'need not resolve' preemption before rejecting the state-law claims on their merits. Is the jurisdictional basis 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (final judgment)? More importantly, is it standard for the court of appeals to bypass a preemption analysis and affirm on any ground supported by the record (even if the district court relied on preemption), and are there constraints on doing so?

questions.title: Why apply Illinois law to the Cameo Terms-of-Service claim if Santos was not a party to that contract?
questions.question_body: The court applied Illinois law (the ToS governing-law clause) to hold Santos wasn’t a third-party beneficiary. How do courts select governing law when the plaintiff is a non-signatory asserting third-party rights? Is it routine to honor the contract’s choice-of-law clause to determine if a third party can enforce it, or is a separate choice-of-law analysis usually required?

questions.title: What made Santos’s implied-in-fact contract theory inadequate under New York law at the pleading stage?
questions.question_body: The panel cites Caniglia and DG & A Management to say Santos failed to plead 'essential terms' and a 'meeting of the minds' that Kimmel would adhere to Cameo’s ToS. What specific terms would need to be pleaded to establish an implied-in-fact promise in this context (e.g., scope of permitted use, commercial restrictions, attribution)? Can industry custom or the platform’s standard practices supply those terms without express assent?

questions.title: Why did the fraudulent inducement claim fail for lack of 'out-of-pocket' loss, and what would count as such a loss here?
questions.question_body: The court, applying Lama Holding and Connaughton, found no actual pecuniary loss. If Santos spent time making the videos and alleges he was tricked into doing so under false pretenses, why isn’t the value of his time or the price differential between a personal Cameo and a commercial broadcast license an out-of-pocket loss? What allegations would satisfy New York’s 'out-of-pocket' rule in a case like this?

questions.title: Could the district court have declined supplemental jurisdiction over the state-law claims after dismissing the federal copyright claims?
questions.question_body: Because the court held the copyright claims barred by fair use at the pleading stage, could (or should) the district court have dismissed the state-law claims without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)? On appeal, does the Second Circuit’s merits affirmance of the state-law dismissals implicitly approve the exercise of supplemental jurisdiction, or is that issue waived/harmless here?

questions.title: How does Melendez’s 'extra element' test for preemption apply to contract-based restrictions on use of copyrighted works?
questions.question_body: The panel avoids deciding preemption but notes Santos’s view that his contract claims are 'qualitatively different.' Under Second Circuit law, when do contractual promises (e.g., not to broadcast commercially, or to limit uses) add the 'extra element' that avoids § 301 preemption? Would specific, bargained-for use restrictions in a ToS or side agreement typically survive preemption if adequately pleaded?

questions.title: Why did the court rely on a 'reasonable observer' perception of the Cameo videos’ original purpose rather than Santos’s own stated intent?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Warhol to discount subjective intent and notes Santos’s own complaint described the videos as conveying 'hope, strength, perseverance, encouragement, and positivity.' How does the 'reasonable observer' approach operate at the pleadings stage when a plaintiff insists his actual purpose matched the defendant’s characterization? Does the court’s ability to view the works themselves override contrary conclusory allegations?

questions.title: Did the court’s finding that defendants aimed to 'comment and criticize' foreclose any secondary liability theories against ABC and Disney?
questions.question_body: The panel affirmed dismissal across the board once fair use applied. If fair use is a complete defense to direct infringement, does that necessarily defeat vicarious/contributory theories against the broadcaster and parent company? Are there scenarios where a secondary-liability theory could survive even if the use is ultimately held fair?

questions.title: Does the possibility that Kimmel could be a co-author or joint author of the videos (by crafting prompts) affect the fair-use analysis?
questions.question_body: Santos argued Kimmel 'designed' the videos’ purpose by submitting the prompts. If, hypothetically, Kimmel’s contributions rose to the level of joint authorship (or an implied license existed), would that change the fair-use calculus, or simply eliminate infringement altogether? How do courts treat authorship or implied-license arguments when the same facts are used to claim the secondary use is non-transformative?
